William the Conqueror died in 1087..why: Common-sense case: people say the year William died (1087); nobody writes that he did not also die in 1090, it is taken for granted that a person dies once. It follows from functionality, so without it the prompt's one year does not exclude another.

sources.quote: He was taken to the priory of Saint Gervase at Rouen, where he died on 9 September 1087.

sources.query: William the Conqueror did not die in 1090

Charlemagne died in 814..why: Common-sense case: 'Charlemagne died in 814' is stated everywhere; that he did not die in 815 as well is never written, it follows from the relation being functional.

sources.quote: Charlemagne died in 814 and was buried at the Palatine Chapel (now part of Aachen Cathedral) in Aachen, his imperial capital city.
Magna Carta (Medieval Latin for "Great Charter"), sometimes spelled Magna Charta, is a royal charter of rights sealed by King John of England at Runnymede, near Windsor, on 15 June 1215.

Abraham Lincoln was the first president.why: Deliberately false so the disjunction turns on the edited property: Lincoln was the 16th president; Washington was the first.

notes: RBox contraction paired with history-replace-0018: removes the revision's ORIGINAL property, that 'died in year' is functional (the revision makes it many-valued). Every query becomes "I don't know", including the three propositional ones (strong Kleene). The instances are the revision's (William I, 1087; Charlemagne, 814), asking whether the stated year rules out a second one: yes while the relation is functional, undetermined after removal. Residual risk, recorded: a person dies once, so a model may answer "yes" from what death means and not from the property; a "yes" is a route around the removal, never a sign it worked. The angle noted for the revision (the edit overrides what death means) applies here too. Near and far unrelated queries are the revision's (near exempt from Rule 7).
